About this citation

The Analects is a compiled record of sayings, not a work by Confucius. The common formula 'Confucius said' refers to a tradent whose words were assembled by later hands, and the book-and-chapter locator is what makes a passage findable in any edition.

Exact wording

English (as recorded here)
“The Master said: Those who know it are not equal to those who love it; those who love it are not equal to those who delight in it.”
Classical Chinese
“知之者不如好之者，好之者不如樂之者。”

The repeated object is 之, a pronoun referring back to the Way. The English has to choose a noun for it, and the choice goes a long way toward deciding what the sentence seems to be about.

Forms in circulation that differ

  • “They who know the truth are not equal to those who love it.”
  • “Those who know the truth are not equal to those who love it.”
  • “The one who knows is not equal to the one who loves.”

Attribution notes

Analects 6.20. The familiar English “they who know the truth” comes from a nineteenth-century translation that expanded the pronoun 之 into “the truth,” and the phrase then travelled as a freestanding aphorism — complete with the “they who” construction that belongs to Victorian English, not to Confucius. The original ranks three relations to the Way: knowing it, loving it, delighting in it. The third stage is the one Confucius puts highest, and it is the one the popular English version drops entirely.

About Confucius

Confucius (Kong Qiu, 551–479 BCE) taught in the late Spring and Autumn period amid the Zhou order’s political fragmentation. Born in the state of Lu, he briefly held local office and then spent years seeking rulers who would adopt ritual-based, virtue-centered government.

Interpretation

Confucius ranks three relations to a pursuit: knowing it, loving it, and delighting in it. The claim is that each is a genuine advance on the previous, and that the last is not intensity but a change in what the activity is for — it has become its own point. In the Analects this belongs to his repeated insistence that learning not be undertaken for external reward. The ranking is a diagnosis of why effort fails.

Why it matters

It gives a way to assess engagement: are you doing this because of what it leads to, or because of the doing? The difference shows under difficulty.

Questions readers arrive with

What is the source of the quotation “The Master said: Those who know it are…”?

“The Master said: Those who know it are…” comes from The Analects, 6.20 (c. 5th–3rd century BCE (compiled)), attributed to Confucius.

What does Confucius mean by learning?

Education is not only information transfer; it is the shaping of attention and character. Confucian learning, Socratic midwifery, and Deweyan growth offer rival models. This passage enters that discussion through learning.

Is the wording of this Confucius quotation commonly changed?

The wording recorded here is “The Master said: Those who know it are not equal to those who love it; those who love it are not equal to those who delight in it.” Forms in circulation that differ: They who know the truth are not equal to those who love it. / Those who know the truth are not equal to those who love it. / The one who knows is not equal to the one who loves. The Classical Chinese reads “知之者不如好之者，好之者不如樂之者。”

Is this quotation attributed correctly?

Analects 6.20. The familiar English “they who know the truth” comes from a nineteenth-century translation that expanded the pronoun 之 into “the truth,” and the phrase then travelled as a freestanding aphorism — complete with the “they who” construction that belongs to Victorian English, not to Confucius. The original ranks three relations to the Way: knowing it, loving it, delighting in it. The third stage is the one Confucius puts highest, and it is the one the popular English version drops entirely.
